newsitem.title: UK: UK government forced onto back foot in food row.
newsitem.headline: UK government forced onto back foot in food row.

text.p: The British government came under new pressure over a food safety scare on Wednesday, forcing Prime Minister John Major to announce an inquiry and Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg to agree to a parliamentary statement.

Hogg bowed to opposition pressure to explain to the House of Commons later on Wednesday what steps his department had taken to make meat safe after the crisis over mad cow disease and a recent food poisoning outbreak in Scotland which killed 20 people.

Officials said Major also ordered a report late on Tuesday from the agriculture ministry on what steps it had taken to deal with the problems and when they had been implemented. The report would be published soon, they said.

But Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown said the competence of Hogg and the government had been called into question by the row and he demanded a full public inquiry into food safety and public health.

"There is now a real danger that the British agriculture and food industries, as well as public health, will suffer serious long-term damage from the lack of public confidence in the government's handling of food safety and public health issues," he said.

"This is a consequence, not only of the lamentable performance of the agriculture minister and his department, but also of the secrecy and evasion that surrounds government statements," Ashdown added in an open letter to Major.
The government is already under fire from the main opposition Labour party, which last week accused it of covering up a report on abattoir standards.

Labour, which is already tipped by polls to win the election Major must hold by May, has vowed to create a Food Standard Agency independent of the agriculture ministry to ensure consumer interests are not sacrificed to those of farmers.
On Tuesday Labour published a letter to junior agriculture minister Angela Browning from Peter Comrie, the Association of Meat Inspectors' general secretary.
Comrie said some inspectors had been threatened for trying to take action over breaches of hygiene in abattoirs and warned that falling standards were creating "a potential timebomb".

Then on Wednesday, Labour consumer affairs spokesman Nigel Griffiths said meat inspection officials in north east England had also written to Hogg last year saying staff shortages meant they could not properly enforce hygiene standards.

Hogg fought back, telling a radio interviewer he had not received the letter. But he rejected suggestions that hygiene standards and controls to stop the spread of mad cow disease -- bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) -- were inadequate.
"Controls... are rigorously and vigorously enforced within the abattoirs by the meat hygiene service whose numbers have been very substantially reinforced," Hogg said on Wednesday.
Hogg also tried to return the fire, accusing Labour of making political capital out of the crisis in the meat industry,
"We are in the last few weeks of this parliament, leading up to a general election. The Labour party are trying to put whatever spin they can on these matters," Hogg said.

But Hogg's defiant stand failed to dispel what political analysts said was an image of muddle in the government's handling of the BSE crisis, which has cost the government 3.5 billion pounds ($5.62 billion) in compensation, and in the food poisoning outbreak.
